reason: The sources provide over 15 verified claims across multiple sites regarding the asteroid's discovery, size, 57-day capture period, and surprising lunar origin.
story: In late 2024, Earth gained a second moon, but it wasn't a new planet—it was a piece of our old one. Discovered by the ATLAS telescope in South Africa, asteroid 2024 PT5 was captured by Earth's gravity on September 29, remaining a temporary satellite for 57 days. Unlike most space rocks, this bus-sized visitor didn't come from the distant asteroid belt. When astronomers at the Gemini North and IRTF telescopes analyzed its light spectrum, they found a 'smoking gun': its chemical signature perfectly matched lunar rock. This rock was likely blasted off the Moon's surface by a massive impact thousands of years ago. Though it never completed a full orbit before escaping back to its 'Arjuna' asteroid family, it left scientists with a rare chance to study Moon debris up close. It won't stay away forever, though; it’s scheduled to return and become our mini-moon again in 2084.
angle: Earth's temporary 'second moon' was actually a long-lost chunk of the Moon itself, blasted into space by a massive impact.

claims.claim: Asteroid 2024 PT5 was discovered on August 7, 2024.
The asteroid was discovered by the ATLAS telescope located in Sutherland, South Africa.
The object is approximately 10 to 11 meters (33 to 37 feet) in diameter.
Earth's gravity captured the object as a temporary satellite on September 29, 2024.
The mini-moon capture period ended on November 25, 2024.
The asteroid remained a temporary moon for approximately 57 days.
The object is composed of ejecta from a massive impact on the Moon.
Its reflectance spectrum matches silicate minerals found in lunar rock samples.
The asteroid belongs to the Arjuna asteroid family or belt.
The object did not complete a full orbit around Earth during its capture.
It follows a horseshoe-shaped orbital path relative to Earth.
The asteroid is too small and dim to be seen with typical backyard telescopes.
It is predicted to return as a mini-moon in the year 2084.
Scientists used solar radiation pressure analysis to prove the object was natural and not human-made debris.
The object was removed from the Sentry Risk Table after being deemed no threat to Earth.
The asteroid made a close approach on January 9, 2025, while traveling at approximately 2,300 mph.

disputed: Minimoon classification: A 2025 study mentioned in S1 argues it should not be called a minimoon because its orbit is dominantly heliocentric, while S3, S4, S6, and S7 explicitly use the term.
2055 capture: S4 suggests that newer data makes a 2055 capture unlikely, while S1, S3, and S6 state it is predicted to occur.
1960 capture: S3 and S7 suggest a potential unnoticed capture event in 1960, but this is presented as a reconstruction rather than an observed fact.
